content: 1. Individuals who have undergone an organ or hematological transplant or those diagnosed with silicosis should be systematically tested and treated for tuberculosis (TB) infection to mitigate the risk of disease progression. 2. Systematic testing and treatment for TB infection may also be considered for high-risk groups such as prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from countries with a high TB burden, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. 3. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, or a persistent cough, or who have been in contact with a person diagnosed with TB, should undergo thorough evaluation for TB and other diseases causing similar symptoms. If TB disease is ruled out following clinical evaluation or national guidelines, these children should be offered TB preventive treatment regardless of their age. 4. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those who do not report symptoms such as a persistent cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have TB disease. However, individuals reporting any of these symptoms should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If TB disease is excluded, they should be offered TB preventive treatment, irrespective of their antiretroviral treatment status. 5. Among adults and adolescents living with HIV, chest X-rays may be utilized as a screening tool for TB disease. 6. C-reactive protein (CRP) levels greater than 5 mg/L may also be used to screen for TB disease in adults and adolescents living with HIV. 7. Molecular diagnostic tests recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) may be employed to screen for TB disease in adults and adolescents living with HIV. 8. For HIV-negative household contacts aged 5 years or older and other at-risk groups, the absence of TB symptoms and normal chest radiographic findings may be used to rule out TB disease before initiating TB preventive treatment. 9. In populations where TB screening is recommended, individuals aged 15 years or older may undergo systematic screening for TB disease using symptom screening, chest X-rays, or molecular diagnostic tests, either alone or in combination. 10. For individuals under 15 years of age who are close contacts of a person with TB, systematic screening for TB disease should include symptom screening (cough, fever, or poor weight gain), chest radiography, or both. 11. Testing for TB infection can be conducted using either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). 12. Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBST) may also be used to test for TB infection. 13. Recommended TB preventive treatment options, regardless of HIV status, include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. 14. Alternative TB preventive treatment options, irrespective of HIV status, include a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or 4 months of daily rifampicin. 15. For individuals exposed to multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB, 6 months of daily levofloxacin should be used as TB preventive treatment. 16. Tuberculosis infection (TBI) is defined as a state of persistent immune response to stimulation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without evidence of clinically manifest TB disease. Approximately one-fourth of the global population is estimated to have been infected with M. tuberculosis. 17. The majority of individuals with TBI are asymptomatic and non-infectious but remain at risk of developing TB disease and becoming infectious. The lifetime risk of progression to TB disease is estimated to be 5–10%, with the highest risk occurring within the first 5 years after initial infection. 18. The risk of TB disease progression is influenced by several factors, with immunological status being the most critical determinant. 19. The WHO End TB Strategy emphasizes the importance of TB preventive treatment (TPT) as a key component in eliminating TB. Between 2024 and 2027, member states have committed to providing TPT to at least 45 million individuals. 20. The efficacy of current TPT regimens ranges from 60% to 90%, but the potential benefits of treatment must be weighed against the risk of drug-related adverse events. 21. Mass, population-wide testing and treatment for TBI are currently not feasible due to imperfect diagnostic tests, the risk of severe adverse drug reactions, and high costs, which may not provide clear benefits for low-risk populations. 22. TPT is more likely to benefit individuals in high-risk groups where the risk of progression to TB disease significantly exceeds that of the general population. 23. For individuals exposed to multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB, providing appropriate TPT may be more justifiable due to the challenges associated with treating drug-resistant TB. 24. Programmatic management of TPT (PMTPT) involves a comprehensive package of interventions, including identifying and testing individuals at risk, delivering effective and safe treatment, ensuring treatment completion, and monitoring and evaluation. 25. PMTPT aligns with broader preventive actions outlined in the WHO End TB Strategy, including TB screening, infection control, prevention and care of HIV and other co-morbidities, access to universal healthcare, social protection, and poverty alleviation. 26. WHO guidelines on TPT are based on the likelihood of TBI progressing to TB disease in specific risk groups, the underlying epidemiology and burden of TB, and the feasibility and public health benefits of the intervention. 27. The guidelines aim to provide a foundation for developing national PMTPT guidelines tailored to local circumstances and to expand TPT coverage, including for individuals exposed to multidrug-resistant TB. 28. The updated guidelines incorporate new evidence and developments, including revised WHO guidance on TB screening and new modalities for TBI testing, as well as findings from landmark trials on TPT for contacts of individuals with multidrug-resistant TB. 29. The guidelines are intended for use by national TB and HIV programs, maternal and child health programs, policymakers, clinicians, and other stakeholders involved in TB prevention and care. 30. The primary beneficiaries of the guidelines are individuals in high-risk groups, including people with HIV, contacts of individuals with TB, and others at increased risk of progression from TBI to TB disease.
